To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have raised a panel of 17 antisera with specificity for myeloblastic antigens and have shown that these antigens are not unique to leukaemic cells.
we found no evidence for the existence of leukaemic-specific cell surface antigens in human myeloblastic cells.

(1) 17/94 antisera raised against human leukaemia myeloblast have activity against at least one leukaemic myelo-blast line; (2) this activity is not leukaemia-specific; (3) the activity of these sera can be removed by absorption with normal human marrow.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for detecting leukaemic-specific cell surface antigens in human leukaemic cells.
a study of the immunological and biochemical nature of the antigens present on the surface of human myeloid leukaemic blasts and normal myeloid precursor cells.
the development of a sensitive assay system for the detection of leukaemic-specific cell surface antigens.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the antisera used in this study do not detect any leukaemia-specific antigens on the surface of myeloblast cell populations.
the sera contain activity against cell surface antigens present on a minority population of marrow cells, but not on leukaemic-specific surface antigens.
these antisera do not contain antibody to any myeloblast-specific antigens.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have failed to produce antisera which are reactive with antigens which are expressed on leukaemic myoblasts but not on normal myeloblast.

the majority of leukaemic myoblasts are immunologically similar to a normal subpopulation of marrow cells and that the leukaemic myeloplastic state is not associated with the development of leukaemic-specific surface antigens.
there are no detectable surface antigens in leukaemic myleoblasts which are not present on a minority population of cells in normal marrow.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of heterologous antispecies in the study of human leukaemic antigens requires extensive absorption with normal human spleen and marrow to remove antibodies directed against normal polymorphic antigens and other non-antileukaemic cell surface antigens.
the use of heterologous antisERA to detect surface antigens on myeloblast is fraught with difficulty and the results obtained are not likely to be of clinical value.
the majority of sera raised against leukaemic blasts have activity against normal marrow and that this activity is not easily removed by absorption with cadaver spleen.
